title: SN 1996cr in Circinus galaxy
caption: The central regions of the Circinus galaxy, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This composite looks into the heart of the nearby Circinus galaxy, about 12 million light-years away according to the caption. A blue source near the lower right corner stands out. It is the supernova SN 1996cr, finally identified more than a decade after it exploded.

Its discovery was a piece of detective work. In 2001 it was singled out as a bright, variable object in a Chandra X-ray image, but its identity as a supernova was only confirmed years later. Clues from a spectrum taken with ESO's Very Large Telescope prompted the team to search through data from 18 different telescopes, on the ground and in space, nearly all of it already sitting in archives.
Among supernovae of the last 25 years, SN 1996cr is one of the closest to us. Old archive data, pieced together, let astronomers reconstruct the history of an explosion nobody noticed at the time.

understand.summary: This composite combines Chandra X-ray data, shown in blue, with Hubble data shown in yellow (I-band), red (hydrogen emission), cyan (V-band) and light blue (oxygen emission).
understand.eye: X-rays are invisible to the eye, and the supernova was bright in X-rays long before anyone recognized it.
